facts.statement: Fossils of the only known species, Eoalligator chunyii, were discovered and described in 1964 alongside the remains of Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
facts.quote: Fossils of the type and only species, Eoalligator chunyii, were first discovered in 1964 and described alongside the bones of Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.

facts.statement: The genus Eoalligator was named in 1964 by Yang Zhongjian based on fossil material collected in Guangdong Province.
facts.quote: The genus Eoalligator was named in 1964 by Yang Zhongjian (also known as C.C. Young) based on assorted fossil material collected in the Guangdong Province

facts.statement: Eoalligator is an extinct crocodilian found in Late Cretaceous to Paleocene sediments of China.
facts.quote: Eoalligator is an extinct genus of alligatoroid crocodilian known from fragmentary remains that have been recovered from Late Cretaceous to Paleocene sediments of China.

facts.statement: Fossils of Eoalligator chunyii come from the Zhenshui Formation (Late Cretaceous) and the Shanghu Formation (Lower Paleocene).
facts.quote: These localities correspond to the Zhenshui Formation (Late Cretaceous), strata thought to date to the K-PG boundary, and the Shanghu Formation (Lower Paleocene).

facts.statement: The original material for Eoalligator chunyii was found in three localities within 8 km of each other in Nanxiong County.
facts.quote: The material assigned to Eoalligator chunyii by Young came exclusively from Nanxiong County, specifically three localities (identified as L1, L2 and L3) all within 8 km of one another.

facts.statement: A second species, Eoalligator huiningensis, was described in 1982 from material found in Anhui Province.
facts.quote: In 1982 Young erected a second species, Eoalligator huiningensis, based on material found in the Wanghudun Formation of the Anhui Province.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Eoalligator chunyii and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis represent the same animal or distinct species.
facts.quote: While one 2016 study eventually suggested that the two might in fact represent the same animal, more recent work has been published arguing that the two are in fact different.

facts.statement: Researchers questioned the validity of Eoalligator huiningensis because the original describer did not compare it to E. chunyii and they lacked shared diagnostic traits.
facts.quote: The team also questioned the referral of E. huiningensis to the genus, highlighting that Young did not compare E. huiningensis to E. chunyii when describing it and that the two did not share any diagnostic traits.

facts.statement: The classification of Eoalligator has shifted over time, moving from alligatorine to crocodyloid and finally to the clade Orientalosuchina.
facts.quote: The relationship between Eoalligator and other crocodilians has repeatedly shifted: it was initially interpreted as an alligatorine, then for some time as a type of crocodyloid before being placed in the clade Orientalosuchina

facts.statement: Eoalligator had a short and blunt snout sharing traits with both crocodyloids and alligatoroids.
facts.quote: Like other orientalosuchins Eoalligator possessed a short and blunt snout that shares characteristics with both crocodyloids and alligatoroids

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Eoalligator shows a pattern of concave and convex regions along the tooth row known as festooning.
facts.quote: The lower margin of the upper jaw displays a clear pattern of concave and convex regions following the toothrow, a condition known as festooning.

facts.statement: The front part of the lower jaw of Eoalligator is short, reaching only as far as the fourth tooth.
facts.quote: The mandibular symphysis, the region at the front of the lower jaw where both mandibles meet, is short and extends only to the level of the fourth tooth of the dentary.

facts.statement: A specific depression on the lower jaw bone is a unique trait shared by Eoalligator and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
facts.quote: The surangular furthermore preserves a depression immediately beside the fossa, a trait shared by Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that a depression on the lower jaw of Eoalligator might become less prominent as the animal grows older.
facts.quote: It has also been noted that this sulcus might be variable across specimens of different ages, as some remains of Eoalligator preserve a much more prominent depression, suggesting that it might grow less and less prominent as the animal grows.

facts.statement: At least four tooth sockets were found in the front of the snout, but damage suggests the fifth socket was destroyed before discovery.
facts.quote: A minimum of four tooth sockets are preserved in each premaxilla of Eoalligator, however as noted in the 2016 revision, the examined specimen was damaged towards the very front of the snout, likely meaning that the front most alveolus was destroyed prior to the fossils discovery.

facts.statement: In the front teeth of Eoalligator, the third tooth is the largest and the fifth is the smallest.
facts.quote: Of these, the third is the largest and the fifth is the smallest.

facts.statement: The upper teeth of Eoalligator are described as blunt with smooth edges, unlike the bulbous teeth of early Globidonta.
facts.quote: Wang and colleagues describe them as blunt with smooth cutting edges and some compression, setting them apart from the very bulbous teeth of most early members of Globidonta.

facts.statement: An early researcher named Young estimated that Eoalligator had 23 teeth in its lower jaw.
facts.quote: Young initially gave an estimated count of 23 dentary teeth.

facts.statement: The fourth tooth in the lower jaw of Eoalligator was likely the largest and fit into a specific socket between the front and upper jaw bones.
facts.quote: As in other orientalosuchins and many crocodilians in general, the fourth appears to have been the largest and would have slid into the fossa present between the premaxilla and maxilla.

facts.statement: The 11th and 12th teeth in the lower jaw of Eoalligator were enlarged, but not as much as the fourth tooth.
facts.quote: The 11th and 12th teeth of the lower jaw are also described as enlarged, though not as much as the fourth.

facts.statement: Eoalligator is described as being of moderate size.
facts.quote: Eoalligator has been described as moderately-sized.

facts.statement: A 2016 study classified Eoalligator as a member of Crocodylidae and suggested it might be the same species as Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
facts.quote: While Eoalligator was originally classified as an extinct relative of alligators, the 2016 revision by Wang and colleagues recovered it as a member of Crocodylidae and as the sister taxon to Asiatosuchus nanlingensis, which they took as support for their hypothesis that the two represented a single species.

facts.statement: A later study disagreed with the idea that Eoalligator and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis are the same species, though both agreed Eoalligator is a crocodyloid.
facts.quote: However, a subsequent study by Wu et al. disagreed with the synonymy of the two, although they agreed in classifying E. chunyii as a crocodyloid.

facts.statement: Eoalligator was reclassified as an alligatoroid when a new group called Orientalosuchina was established.
facts.quote: Eoalligator returned to its original placement as an alligatoroid with the recognition of Orientalosuchina later that year, named by Massonne et al. alongside their description of Orientalosuchus.

facts.statement: Recent studies place Eoalligator as the closest relative to the Cretaceous crocodilian Jiangxisuchus.
facts.quote: In these studies, Eoalligator was again placed as the sister taxon to Jiangxisuchus, similar to the results of Li and colleagues.

facts.statement: A 2024 study raised doubts about whether the group Orientalosuchina, which includes Eoalligator, is truly an alligatoroid or more closely related to crocodyloids.
facts.quote: This interpretation is not uncontested. Some doubt over Massonne's idea of Orientalosuchina was cast by a 2024 study on the osteology Crocodylus palaeindicus, which remarked on how the placement of the clade within Alligatoroidea might not be wholly supported and that they could represent a group more closely allied with crocodyloids.

facts.statement: Researchers acknowledge that the alternative classification placing Orientalosuchina within Mekosuchinae has relatively weak support and needs more study.
facts.quote: However, support for this particular topology is acknowledged as being relatively weak, though deserving of further study.

facts.statement: Fossils of Eoalligator have been found in multiple locations within China's Nanxiong Basin.
facts.quote: Material of Eoalligator is known from several localities throughout China's Nanxiong Basin

facts.statement: Eoalligator fossils from the Shanghu Formation date to after the K-PG extinction event.
facts.quote: The records of Eoalligator from the Shanghu Formation are younger, having been preserved following the K-PG extinction

facts.statement: Eoalligator belongs to the parent group Orientalosuchina.
facts.quote: Parent group: Orientalosuchina

facts.statement: Eoalligator is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Eoalligator is Eoalligator chunyii.
facts.quote: Type species: Eoalligator chunyii

facts.statement: Eoalligator lived between 60.9 and 57.5 million years ago during the Selandian to Thanetian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Thanetian (60.9 to 57.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Eoalligator in the Paleobiology Database.
